metadata.title: Gastric cancer and ulcerative colitis in East Asians: a genetic association study - analysis code and derived results
metadata.description:
Analysis code, derived variant-level inputs, and result tables for the manuscript
"Gastric cancer and ulcerative colitis in East Asians: a genetic association study"
(Kim JE, Lee H, Oh YE, Kim TS, Min YW, Min BH, Lee JH, Rhee PL).

This archive allows every number reported in the manuscript and in Online Resource 1
to be checked, and allows the analyses to be re-executed from publicly available
genome-wide association study summary statistics. Full genome-wide summary statistics
are not redistributed, because the source databases license them directly to users.

Contents: analysis scripts in R and Python and one Colab notebook; derived variant-level
inputs; all output tables and execution logs; main figures 1-4 and supplementary figure
S2 at 600 dpi and as vector PDF; and a table mapping each analytical output to the
corresponding result in the article and in Online Resource 1.

The study screened 12 East Asian immune-phenotype datasets against gastric cancer,
partitioned the ulcerative colitis instrument into variants inside and outside the
extended major histocompatibility complex, tested regional overlap at HLA-DQA1/DQB1,
and examined associations with other diseases. Analyses used summary statistics from
IEU OpenGWAS and the GWAS Catalog. No individual-level data were used.

See README.md in the archive for data sources, reproduction steps, the output-to-manuscript
mapping, random seeds, and known limitations.

metadata.title: From Libraries To Digital Platforms: Information Source Use Among Engineering Students In Erode District, Tamil Nadu
metadata.description: The rapid growth of digital technologies has significantly changed the information-seeking behaviour of engineering students. While traditional library resources continue to play an important role, digital platforms such as e-books, e-journals, institutional repositories, and online databases have become essential sources of academic information. This study examines the information source use of engineering college students in Erode District, Tamil Nadu, during the academic year 2016–2017. A descriptive survey research design was adopted, and data were collected from 250 undergraduate engineering students selected. Stratified random sampling method was adopted for sample selection. A structured questionnaire based on a five-point Likert scale was used to collect primary data from the students’ community. The study investigates the influence of department, year of study, and parents' educational qualification on the use of library books, reference books, printed journals, e-books, and e-journals. Data are analysed using descriptive statistics (frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation, and ranking) and inferential statistics (One-way ANOVA and Chi-square test). The findings are expected to assist the librarians and academic administrators in strengthening library collections and digital information services to meet the changing information needs of engineering students.

metadata.title: Harmonized Drug Dataset (HDD)
metadata.description: Harmonized Drug Dataset (abbreviated as HDD) integrates comprehensive metadata for small‑molecule compounds, combining structural, physicochemical, regulatory, toxicological, and experimental assay information from PubChem, LINCS, Cell Painting, DeepChem resources, and multiple toxicology databases. It includes curated binding affinities, bioassay outcomes, adverse drug reactions, toxicity measurements, and machine‑learning‑ready molecular fingerprints. The dataset is designed to support large‑scale modeling, compound characterization, and toxicology prediction workflows.

metadata.title: Reproducibility Package for Point-in-Time Validity in Municipal 311 Service-Time Prediction: A Multi-City Benchmark of Outcome Construction, Information Availability, and Temporal Evaluation
metadata.description: This record contains the reproducibility package for the study “Point-in-Time Validity in Municipal 311 Service-Time Prediction: A Multi-City Benchmark of Outcome Construction, Information Availability, and Temporal Evaluation.” The study evaluates how outcome-model specification, point-in-time information availability, and temporal evaluation affect municipal 311 service-time prediction across Austin, Chicago, and New York City. The benchmark crossed closed-only squared-error regression and cutoff-censored Normal accelerated failure-time modelling, creation-stable and hindsight information contracts, and random retrospective and rolling-origin evaluation protocols. The package includes the complete Supporting Information, a machine-readable supporting-data workbook, CSV exports, analysis and audit scripts, dated protocol and environment locks, extraction and cohort manifests, aggregated primary and secondary results, calibration-resolution outputs, model-ranking and practical-tie analyses, sanitized portal metadata snapshots, file manifests, and SHA-256 checksums. The primary benchmark comprises 120 factorial result cells. The secondary and sensitivity analyses comprise 136 additional cells. The package also includes the numerical-integrity audit used to resolve 180 primary calibration-slope estimates. Raw municipal request records, request identifiers, request-level predictions, fitted model objects, feature-table files, databases, virtual environments, and execution logs are not redistributed. The official municipal open-data portals remain the sources of record. Extraction manifests and reconstruction scripts are provided, but later re-extraction may not produce byte-identical source files if the municipal portals revise historical records. The prediction outcome is time to an administrative terminal disposition recorded by the municipal system. It should not be interpreted as verified physical resolution of the reported issue. The outcome and evaluation contrasts compare complete benchmark specifications and should not be interpreted as isolated causal effects of censoring or random splitting. The hindsight information contract is diagnostic and includes mutable current-state fields and near-terminal proxies that were unavailable at request creation.

metadata.title: TRUSTEX Poster: Digital Product Passports for Circular Textiles
metadata.description:
Poster presented at the DPP4EU event by Jérome Dierickx (TerraMatters), Elena Hidalgo (CETIM Technological Centre), David Ariza (CETIM Technological Centre), and Beatriz Mafra (Made2Flow), 22 May 2026.

This poster presents the approach of the Horizon Europe project TRUSTEX ("Advancing Sustainable Textiles in the Circular Economy through Innovative EPR Schemes") to Digital Product Passports (DPPs) for textiles. It addresses a core barrier: the textile sector combines fragmented supply chains with a shortage of harmonised standards, which makes it difficult to collect and exchange the information a DPP requires. TRUSTEX develops interoperable digital infrastructures that turn fragmented and heterogeneous data into standardised, regulation-ready outputs.

The methods build on the Product Circularity Data Sheet (PCDS, ISO 59040), which communicates circularity attributes such as recycled content, repairability, and end-of-life options in interoperable formats and supports ESPR compliance, while noting that taxonomy gaps and sector-specific complexities remain unresolved. The workflow moves from data collection at brands and suppliers, through terminology mapping and PCDS data alignment, to a backend database, a blockchain layer, and a user interface that presents DPP information to the final user. Participants hold dynamic roles, for example manufacturer, waste manager, and final user, with restricted access so that only verified participants add data and only authorised users assign roles, which guards against fraudulent entries.

The key innovations combine standardised APIs that integrate emission-factor databases, life cycle assessment engines, and verified batch-level supply chain data; AI-driven data validation paired with blockchain trust mechanisms that detect inconsistencies and complement missing information with industry-verified secondary sources; and a blockchain architecture that records a cryptographic fingerprint of the data instead of the data itself, so tampering becomes detectable without exposing confidential business information. Role-based access control limits each participant to their area of responsibility.

The conclusion sets out four design goals for DPP success: data maturity alignment, one-way protection through hashing, double-entry prevention, and universal access via the ERC-1155 standard for compatibility across textile applications. The poster argues that digitalisation is a fundamental requirement for overcoming current barriers to DPP adoption in the sector.

metadata.title: Polymer-grade propylene production through temperature swing adsorption: Molecular simulation and techno-economic analysis
metadata.description: Producing polymer-grade propylene from the propylene-rich mixtures can be quite challenging since the most commonly employed technology, distillation, requires high-energy input and is expensive. Therefore, identifying less-costly, efficient, and environmentally friendly methods, such as the use of the adsorptive process, is highly desirable. In this regard, six pure silica zeolites (AFV, AST, AVL, IFR, LEV, and SWY) as propane selective adsorbents are investigated for the separation of 10 mol.% propane and 90 mol.% propylene mixture. Molecular simulation Monte Carlo (MC) is used to calculate framework structure parameters such as pore volume, surface area, and framework density of pure silica zeolites. Also, adsorption isotherms, propane selectivity, and working capacity are presented using MC calculations. The Langmuir-Freundlich isotherm model is utilized to calculate isotherm parameters. A system model is implemented in Aspen Adsorption software (version 11) and breakthrough curves are achieved. The Temperature Swing Adsorption (TSA) cycle is simulated and key performance parameters such as propylene purity, recovery, and productivity for all six silica zeolites are calculated. Finally, economic analysis of the TSA process is performed using the Aspen Capital Cost Estimator (version 11) and Aspen Process Economic Analyzer (version 11) and compared with the cost of the conventional distillation process. Results showed that the capital cost and operating cost of temperature swing adsorption are 42.3 % and 91.37 % less than those of distillation, respectively.

metadata.title: Polaris - A multi-database literature review system
metadata.description:
POLARIS is an R (Shiny) application designed to streamline multi-database literature searches and export results in RIS format, fully compatible with tools such as Zotero, Mendeley, and EndNote. It was built to support reproducible, large-scale research workflows. Polaris enhances the audibility and transparency of the evidence synthesis process, thereby improving the traceability of the literature review workflow.

🔎 Multi-database search

Run queries across major academic databases, including PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Semantic Scholar.

📄 Standardized export

All results are exported as .ris files, ensuring seamless integration with reference managers such as Zotero, Mendeley, and EndNote.

📊 Search logging

Each search generates a structured results_log.csv, allowing you to track queries, monitor results, and document execution status for reproducibility.

🗂️ Structured outputs

Results can be automatically organized into folders based on query groups, making it easier to manage large-scale literature reviews.

⚡ Performance-focused execution

POLARIS is designed for efficiency, with batch processing, built-in rate limiting, retry handling, and a background worker system that keeps the Shiny interface responsive during long runs.

🎯 Use Cases

POLARIS is particularly useful for:

  • Systematic literature reviews
  • Meta-analyses
  • Evidence synthesis workflows
  • Academic research pipelines

⚙️ Requirements

To run POLARIS, you will need:

  • R ≥ 4.0
  • RStudio (recommended)
  • Elsevier API Key and Institutional Token (required for Scopus and ScienceDirect)

Why POLARIS?

Literature searches are often fragmented, manual, and difficult to reproduce—especially when combining multiple databases, each with its own interface, limitations, and export formats.

POLARIS addresses these challenges by bringing everything into a single environment. It unifies search workflows, automates large-scale query execution, and ensures reproducibility through structured logging and standardized outputs.

Instead of switching between platforms and manually consolidating results, POLARIS allows you to run, monitor, and export your entire search strategy from one place, making it especially powerful for systematic reviews and data-intensive research projects.

metadata.title: ConVer-G: A Suite for Versioning, Querying and Visualization of Dynamic Knowledge Graphs
metadata.description:
A Knowledge Graph (KG) is a structured representation of facts where entities are connected by typed relationships, typically encoded using the Resource Description Framework (RDF) standard. KGs are widely used across domains such as life sciences, urban planning, and weather forecasting, but evolve continuously as data is updated, corrected, and expanded. Managing this evolution through explicit versioning—much like Git does for source code—is essential for reproducibility, auditability, provenance tracking, and temporal analysis.

ConVer-G (Concurrent Versioning of Knowledge Graphs) is a software suite designed to address these challenges by providing snapshot-based version management for RDF datasets [@gil2024convergconcurrentversioningknowledge]. It allows users to ingest successive states of an RDF dataset, query any past version using the standard SPARQL query language, compare versions, and visually inspect how the graph and its history evolve. The suite is composed of three modular and interoperable components:

  1. Quads-loaDer: A command-line interface and service for ingesting RDF data, and storing versioned quads efficiently.
  2. Quads-Query: A query translation engine that converts SPARQL queries into SQL, enabling the interrogation of specific graph versions as well as cross-snapshot and temporal analyses directly over a relational backend.
  3. Quads-Visualizer: A web-based visualization tool that allows users to explore both the metagraph—capturing the structural history of versions, branches, and their ancestry—and the versioned graph, which represents the RDF quads contained in a selected snapshot.

Together, these components implement a condensed snapshot-based representation of RDF graphs that optimizes storage by sharing common quads across versions, while simultaneously supporting concurrent workflows such as branching and merging.

metadata.title: Tendencias históricas de la superación profesional del especialista en Medicina Familiar
metadata.description: La superación profesional constituye un resultado práctico demandado en la investigación educativa. Esta investigación tuvo como objetivo analizar, mediante una revisión documental, las tendencias históricas del desarrollo del proceso de superación profesional del especialista en Medicina Familiar para la atención al adulto con dispepsia. Se realizó una investigación exploratoria entre septiembre de 2022 y junio de 2024. Se utilizaron los métodos teóricos: histórico-lógico, analítico-sintético e inductivo-deductivo. Se utilizaron bases de datos como Redalyc, Redined, Scopus y Scielo. El punto de inflexión tendencial fue 1988 a partir de la primera versión del programa de especialización. Las etapas reveladas transitaron desde los inicios de la superación profesional (1987-2002), su extensión para el diagnóstico gastroscópico en el primer nivel de atención (2002-2019) hasta un retorno a la superación profesional para la atención a las enfermedades digestivas (2019-2025). Se concluyó en un disabalance entre ellas a pesar de sus nexos interdisciplinares e interculturales.

metadata.title: Hygrocybe pseudohypohaemacta Angelini, Dovana, Lodge, M. Marchetti & Vizzini 2026, sp. nov.
metadata.description:
Hygrocybe pseudohypohaemacta Angelini, Dovana, Lodge, M. Marchetti & Vizzini sp. nov.

Figs 11, 12, 13

Etymology.

The specific epithet is derived from the Greek prefix pseudo- (false), referring to its close morphological similarity to H. hypohaemacta, with which it may be easily confused.

Diagnosis.

Differing from H. hypohaemacta in larger microspores, differently shaped macrospores, absence of hymenial cystidia, geographic range, and divergence in ribosomal sequences.

Types.

Dominican Republic, Puerto Plata, Sosúa, loc. Cemetery 19.746151, –70.540367, 23 December 2016, C. Angelini, JBSD 141878 Holotype (ANGE 819 Isotype). GenBank: ITS = PZ 148603, LSU = PZ 145854.

Description.

Pileus 15–28 mm diam., at first and for a long time conical or hemispherical, later expanded to applanate, without an umbo and the margin not or very slightly lobed; surface smooth, glutinous and shiny, with translucent-striate margin up to more than half the radius, uniformly colored bright scarlet red or orange, but always with a narrow yellow margin, some yellow with a reddish-orange center and yellow margin. Lamellae narrowly adnate, just free or sometimes slightly emarginate, ventricose, up to 2 mm broad, intercalated with 2 lengths of lamellulae, white, rarely pale pinkish-orange-red, thick, and distant, with irregular and concolorous edge. Stipe 30–60 × 1–4 mm, cylindrical, straight or curved, often tapered towards the apex, usually partly golden-yellow, sometimes reddish-yellow or reddish orange; surface covered by a very thick transparent glutinous layer (as in Roridomyces Rexer, Mycenaceae Overeem). Context thin, reddish white in the pileus, yellowish white in the stipe. Odor and taste indistinct.

Basidiospores dimorphic; macrospores (7.5 –) 8.2– 9.1 – 9.9 (– 11.0) × (6.0 –) 7.0– 7.8 – 8.7 (– 9.5) µm [246 10 / 6] Q = 1.07– 1.16 – 1.26, V = 214– 300 – 385 µm 3, subglobose to broadly ellipsoid, inamyloid, thin- to thick-walled (wall up to 0.5 µm thick), hyaline, mostly with guttulate content and with a large central guttula; microspores (4.2 –) 4.8– 5.3 – 5.9 (– 6.4) × (3.2 –) 3.8– 4.4 – 5.0 (– 5.6) µm [141 / 10 / 5], Q = 1.09– 1.22 – 1.35, V = 35– 56 – 78 µm 3, subglobose to broadly ellipsoid, inamyloid, thin- to thick-walled (wall up to XX thick µm), hyaline, with only a large central guttula or multiguttulate. Basidia dimorphic; macrobasidia (23.8 –) 27.7– 31.3 – 35.6 (– 39.5) × (8.4 –) 9.5– 10.5 – 11.6 (– 12.6) [33 / 3 / 2], Q = 2.6– 3.0 – 3.4, V = 1398– 1860 – 2322 μm 3, clavate, usually squat, with or without peduncle, thin-walled or slightly thick-walled at apex, hyaline, with guttulate content, tetrasporic and bisporic; sterigmata up to 8 μm long; microbasidia (15.7 –) 18.8– 21.9 – 25.0 (– 28.5) × (4.4 –) 5.2– 6.0 – 6.8 (– 7.6) μm [141 / 10 / 5], Q = 3.1– 3.7 – 4.2, V = 286– 429 – 573 µm 3, narrowly clavate to clavate, mostly with a more or less long peduncle, thin-walled or slightly thick-walled at apex, hyaline, with guttulate content, tetrasporic to bisporic, sterigmata up to 7 μm long. The ratio between macrobasidia and microbasidia varies across different collections. Pleurocystidia and cheilocystidia absent. Lamellar edge fertile with pseudocystidia arising deep in the hymenophoral trama. Pseudocystidia 15–40 (– 50) × 4–6.5 μm, abundant, clavate to subcylindrical, usually sinuous, mostly septate, sometimes bifurcated, with rounded to acute apex, sometimes subcapitate, sometimes with crystalline deposits in the apical portion, thin-walled, hyaline, with smooth or minutely guttulous content. Hymenophoral trama regular to subregular, consisting of parallel hyphae usually> 200 µm long and 5–20 μm wide, thin-walled, hyaline; occasional thromboplerous hyphae with refractive greenish content are present. Pileipellis as an irregular ixotrichoderm, hyphae erect to semi-erect, parallel to intertwined, 2–5 μm wide, frequently exceeding 200 µm in length and multi-articulate (pluriseptate), hyaline, to pale yellowish, terminal elements sometimes enlarged at apex or clavate. Subcutis subregular, hyphae frequently exceeding 200 µm in length, 3–15 (– 30) μm wide, thin-walled, with a pale yellowish cytoplasmic pigment and crystalline deposits. Stipitipellis a mixed ixocutis-ixotrichodermium with abundant gelatinous matrix, consisting of parallel or slightly intertwined hyphae, some over 200 µm long, scarcely septate, 2–7 μm wide, thin- to slightly thick-walled (wall up to 1.0 (– 1.5) μm thick), hyaline or with a pale yellowish cytoplasmic pigment; especially in the apical portion of the stipe, dense tufts of erect, semi-erect interwoven hyphae in gelled material, with a morphology similar to pileal elements. Stipititrama regular to subregular, gelatinized some over 200 µm long, 5–15 (– 20) μm wide, scarcely septate, thin-walled, showing a pale yellowish cytoplasmic pigment and crystalline deposits on the outside. Clamp-connections present throughout.

Habit, habitat, occurrence, and distribution.

Growing gregariously, in groups of a few to many specimens, on litter in broad-leaved forests, sometimes near burned ground (charcoal-pit residue), a few kilometers from the sea. Apparently uncommon and localized. Thus far known from the Dominican Republic, Belize, and French Guiana based on molecular data.

Additional specimens examined.

BELIZE, Orange Walk District, La Milpa Field Station, Lagunita Trail, lat. 17.84, long. – 89.02, 26 October 2002, D. J. Lodge & B. Ortiz-Santana, DJL -BZ-105, CFMR BZ-1903, GenBank U 435150; BRH; CFMR. DOMINICAN REPUBLIC, Puerto Plata, Sosúa, loc. Cemetery 19.746151, –70.540367, 25 December 2016, C. Angelini, JBSD 141874 (ANGE 823 duplicate) ibidem, 25 December 2016, C. Angelini (ANGE 822); ibidem, 25 December 2016, C. Angelini (ANGE 824); ibidem, 25 December 2016, C. Angelini (ANGE 825).

Notes.

Hygrocybe pseudohypohaemacta is characterized by its small-sized, entirely slimy basidiomata; a vivid scarlet-red or orange pileus with a yellow, striate margin; and a stipe covered with a thick, transparent, glutinous layer. Pseudocystidia 15–40 (– 50) × 4–6.5 μm, abundant, clavate to subcylindrical, usually sinuous, mostly septate, sometimes bifurcated, with a rounded to acute apex, sometimes subcapitate, sometimes with crystalline deposits in the apical portion, thin-walled, hyaline, with smooth or minutely guttulate contents. Six sequences of H. pseudohypohaemacta generated in this study, together with two sequences from Belize and French Guiana, formed a well-supported clade (SH-aLRT = 100, UFB = 100, BPP = 1) closely related to H. variecolor. Hygrocybe pseudohypohaemacta, H. variecolor, and other accessions identified as H. aff. / cf. hypohaemacta and Hygrocybe sp. clustered within a well-supported section Velosae clade (SH-aLRT = 100, UFB = 100, BPP = 1), together with H. hypohaemacta, H. snigdha K. P. D. Latha & P. Haridev and H. pellucida K. P. D. Latha & Haridev.

H. pseudohypohaemacta is morphologically close to H. hypohaemacta, but it is well separated in the phylogeny. The nrLSU sequence of H. hypohaemacta from Malaysia (KUM 61079, GenBank KF 381551) showed 93 % identity (492 / 529) with 8 gaps out of 529 (1 %) compared with H. pseudohypohaemacta (ANGE 819) and a patristic distance of 0.34 in the phylogenetic analysis. Based on the original description, the similar H. hypohaemacta differs in having smaller microspores [4–5 × 3–3.5 vs. mostly (4.8 –) 5.3–5.9 × 3.8–5.0 µm], differently shaped macrospores (ovoid to broadly ellipsoid vs. globose, subglobose to broadly ellipsoid), cheilocystidia and caulocystidia at the extreme apex of the stipe, a distribution in Malaysia (Singapore, Corner 1936), and a different nrLSU sequence. Hygrocybe hypohaemacta was also reported from Venezuela and Martinique (Pegler 1983), Puerto Rico (Lodge and Pegler 1990), and Panama (Lodge and Ovrebo 2008) based on morphological data.

The nrITS and nrLSU sequences from the Belize collection named H. hypohaemacta DJL - BZ-105 (Lodge and Ovrebo 2008) were excluded from the phylogenetic analysis. These sequences showed high BLAST similarity to Termitomyces species, indicating that they represent contaminants.

The nrITS sequence of Hygrocybe sp. (ANGE 436, Fig. 11 A) showed 94.41 % identity (474 / 501), with 19 gaps out of 501 (3.7 %), compared with H. pseudohypohaemacta (JBSD 141878, holotype, ANGE 819), and a patristic distance of 0.0093 in the phylogenetic analysis of nrITS and nrLSU. Although the two taxa are morphologically overlapping (data not included), the observed genetic distance and percentage of gaps warrant caution. Therefore, further collections and additional sequences are needed to clarify its taxonomic status and determine whether this taxon represents a distinct species or falls within the variability of H. pseudohypohaemacta.

Comparison of the sequences of H. variecolor (JBSD 141875) with those of H. pseudohypohaemacta (CFMR BZ-1903, GenBank EU 435150) revealed 91 % identity (117 / 129) for the nrITS 1 region, with 3 / 129 gaps (2 %); 84 % identity (132 / 157) for the ITS 2 region, with 15 / 157 gaps (9 %); and 96 % identity (804 / 840) for the nrLSU region, with 13 / 840 gaps (1 %). The data reveal a clear pattern of sequence divergence, with the highest identity in the more conserved nrLSU region (96 %), followed by nrITS 1 (91 %), and the lowest identity in the ITS 2 region (84 %). Conversely, the percentages of gaps show an inverse trend, with ITS 2 exhibiting the highest proportion of gaps (9 %), followed by nrITS 1 (2 %), and nrLSU exhibiting the lowest proportion (1 %). This pattern aligns with the generally accepted understanding of the evolutionary rates of these regions, in which the ITS region, particularly the ITS 2 subregion in this case, tends to evolve more rapidly than the nrLSU gene. Considering the typical thresholds used in fungal taxonomy, the ITS data, with 91 % identity in nrITS 1 and 84 % identity in ITS 2, strongly suggest that H. variecolor and H. pseudohypohaemacta should be considered distinct species. These identity values fall below the commonly cited 97 % threshold for the entire ITS region (Nilsson et al. 2008) and significantly below the higher thresholds suggested for certain genera. The substantial number of gaps, especially in ITS 2, further supports this conclusion. Although the nrLSU region shows a higher identity of 96 %, which is expected given its more conserved nature, it remains below the stringent 99.8 % threshold proposed for species delimitation in some studies of filamentous fungi (Vu et al. 2019).
